title: Reproducibility & Determinism in Tests
summary: A test you can't reproduce isn't a test — it's a rumor. For agents you push toward determinism by pinning the model name and version, setting temperature 0 and any available seed, and recording tool outputs so you can replay them or mock the model entirely. Yet bit-exact reproducibility stays elusive: floating-point nondeterminism, shifting provider infrastructure, and silent model updates mean even temperature 0 isn't a guarantee.

subtopics.title: Determinism is what makes a test meaningful
subtopics.explanation: A test only has value if the same inputs produce the same result, so a failure points at a real change rather than random noise. Agents are probabilistic by default, so a flaky test can't tell you whether your code broke or the model just rolled differently. Pushing toward determinism is what lets a red test mean 'something regressed' instead of 'try again'.
subtopics.example:
# non-deterministic: same input, different outputs
out_a = agent.run("summarize")   # 'A brief summary.'
out_b = agent.run("summarize")   # 'Here is a short recap.'
assert out_a == out_b            # flaky: fails at random

# the goal: pin enough that repeated runs match, so a
# failure signals a real regression, not RNG

subtopics.title: Pin model, version, seed, and temperature
subtopics.explanation: The first lever is removing the obvious sources of variation: name the exact model and its dated version, set temperature to 0 to take the highest-probability token, and pass a fixed seed where the provider supports one. Pinning the version matters most because a silent provider upgrade changes behavior even when your code is untouched. These pins don't guarantee identical bytes, but they collapse most of the variance you can actually control.
subtopics.example:
config = {
    "model": "gpt-x-2026-05-01",   # exact dated version, not a moving alias
    "temperature": 0,               # greedy decoding, least random
    "seed": 42,                     # honored where the provider supports it
    "top_p": 1,
}
# pinning the DATED version guards against silent upgrades that
# change behavior with zero code changes on your side

subtopics.title: Record and replay tool outputs
subtopics.explanation: Agents call tools whose results vary — an API returns live data, a clock advances, a search index changes — so even a pinned model produces different runs. You record each tool's real output once (a cassette/fixture) and replay it on later runs so the environment is frozen. Record/replay is what turns an agent test that depends on the outside world into a self-contained, repeatable unit.
subtopics.example:
CASSETTE = {}   # tool_call -> recorded result

def run_tool(name, args, record=False):
    key = (name, tuple(sorted(args.items())))
    if record:
        CASSETTE[key] = real_tool(name, args)   # capture once
    return CASSETTE[key]                         # replay thereafter

# first pass records live data; every later run replays the
# exact same tool outputs, freezing the environment

subtopics.title: Mock the model to test your own logic
subtopics.explanation: When the thing under test is your orchestration — routing, parsing, retry, the loop — not the generation quality, you replace the model with a stub returning canned responses. A mock is perfectly deterministic and free, so those tests run fast and never flake. Mocking is the right tool whenever the model's cleverness is irrelevant to the behavior you're asserting.

subtopics.title: Bit-exact reproducibility is still elusive
subtopics.explanation: Even with every pin, identical bytes aren't guaranteed: floating-point operations on GPUs are not associative and vary with batching and hardware, provider infrastructure shifts under you, and models get silently updated or deprecated. So temperature 0 reduces variance but does not make output deterministic across time or machines. Accepting this is why robust agent tests assert on tolerances and semantic equivalence rather than exact string matches.
subtopics.example:
# temperature 0 is NOT a determinism guarantee across time/hardware
# fragile:
assert out == "The total is 42.0."

# robust: assert meaning/structure within tolerance
import json
data = json.loads(extract_json(out))
assert data["total"] == 42.0        # value, not exact phrasing
# and gate scores on a tolerance band, never exact equality

foundations.overview: Reproducibility is the property that makes a test trustworthy: run it twice on the same inputs and get the same answer, so a failure means something changed. Agents fight this because LLMs are probabilistic and depend on an external world. You push toward determinism with a stack of controls — pin the exact dated model version so a silent provider upgrade can't shift behavior, set temperature to 0 for greedy decoding, pass a seed where supported, record tool outputs so live APIs and clocks are frozen and replayed, and mock the model outright when you're testing your own orchestration rather than generation quality. Each control removes a source of variance you can actually govern. But bit-exact reproducibility remains out of reach: floating-point math on accelerators isn't associative and varies with batching and hardware, provider infrastructure changes silently, and models are updated or deprecated without notice, so even temperature 0 is not a determinism guarantee across time or machines. The practical consequence is that good agent tests assert on semantics and tolerances — the structured value, the chosen tool, a score within a band — rather than exact byte-for-byte strings, and they treat the pins as variance reduction, not a promise of identical output.
foundations.formalDefinition: Reproducibility in agent testing is the degree to which repeated runs on identical inputs yield identical (or equivalent) outputs. It is approached by pinning the model name and dated version, decoding parameters (temperature 0, seed, top_p), and freezing the environment via record/replay of tool outputs or by mocking the model; bit-exact determinism is generally unattainable due to non-associative floating-point on accelerators, shifting provider infrastructure, and silent model updates, so tests assert semantic/tolerance equivalence rather than exact equality.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without reproducibility, a failing agent test can't distinguish a real regression from random noise, so the whole eval and CI apparatus loses its meaning. Determinism controls are what make a red build actionable and a green build trustworthy, and understanding their limits is what keeps you from writing brittle exact-match assertions that flake forever.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of pins as sandbagging a river: temperature 0, a fixed version, a seed, and replayed tool outputs each block a channel of variance, and together they hold back most of the flood. But the ground itself shifts — floating-point and provider infra move under you — so you can never fully seal it, which is why you build on tolerances rather than assuming the water will never get through.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Teams record VCR-style tool cassettes for agent integration tests, mock the model for fast deterministic loop/routing tests, pin dated model versions in config so a provider bump is an explicit change, and write assertions on parsed values or tolerance bands instead of exact strings so temperature-0 nondeterminism doesn't flake CI.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Setting temperature to 0 makes the model deterministic.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It makes decoding greedy, which reduces variance, but floating-point nondeterminism, batching, hardware differences, and silent provider updates mean the exact output can still change across time and machines.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Pinning the model name is enough to reproduce results later.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A name like 'gpt-x' is often a moving alias that upgrades silently. You must pin the exact dated version, and even then provider infrastructure and deprecations can shift behavior.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Reproducibility means asserting the exact output string.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Because bit-exact output isn't guaranteed, robust tests assert on semantics and tolerances — the parsed value, the chosen tool, a score within a band — not byte-for-byte equality.

interactiveWidget.title: The determinism stack — and where it leaks
interactiveWidget.caption: Each control removes a channel of variance, but the bottom layer never fully seals. Read top-down: what you pin, and the leak it can't stop.

config.note:
REPRODUCIBILITY STACK (most controllable at top)

1. Mock the model
   - Fully deterministic, free, fast.
   - Use when testing YOUR logic (routing, parsing, the loop), not generation quality.
   - Leak: proves nothing about the real model's behavior.

2. Record / replay tool outputs (cassettes)
   - Freezes live APIs, clocks, and search indexes so the environment is repeatable.
   - Leak: stale cassettes drift from reality; you must re-record deliberately.

3. Pin decoding: temperature 0, seed, top_p 1
   - Greedy decoding + seed collapse most sampling variance.
   - Leak: seed is best-effort per provider; temperature 0 is NOT a determinism guarantee.

4. Pin the EXACT dated model version (not a moving alias)
   - Guards against silent provider upgrades that change behavior with zero code changes.
   - Leak: versions get deprecated; provider infra still shifts under you.

5. The floor: floating-point + infrastructure
   - GPU float ops are non-associative and vary with batching/hardware.
   - Bit-exact repro across time and machines is generally UNATTAINABLE.

CONSEQUENCE: assert on semantics and tolerances (parsed value, chosen tool, score within a band) -- never on exact byte-for-byte strings.

checkpoints.prompt: Does setting temperature to 0 make an LLM's output deterministic?
options: Yes, temperature 0 guarantees identical bytes every time
No — it makes decoding greedy and reduces variance, but floating-point, hardware, and silent provider updates can still change the output
Only if you also set top_p to 0
Yes, but only for GPT models
checkpoints.explanation: Temperature 0 selects the highest-probability token (greedy), which cuts sampling variance, but non-associative GPU floating-point, batching/hardware differences, and silent model updates mean the exact output isn't guaranteed across time or machines.

checkpoints.prompt: When should you mock the model entirely in an agent test?
options: When you want to measure the model's answer quality
When the test targets your own logic — routing, parsing, retry, the loop — rather than generation quality
Only in production, never in CI
checkpoints.explanation: A mock returns canned responses, making the test fully deterministic, fast, and free. That's exactly right when you're asserting on orchestration behavior, not on how good the model's generation is.

checkpoints.prompt: This agent test flakes even though temperature is 0. Why?
checkpoints.code:
resp = model.complete(prompt, temperature=0)
assert resp == "The order total is 42.00 USD."   # exact string
options: It asserts an exact byte-for-byte string; temperature 0 isn't a determinism guarantee, so phrasing can vary and the exact match flakes
checkpoints.explanation: Temperature 0 reduces but doesn't eliminate variance, so exact phrasing can shift across runs, hardware, or a silent model update. Assert on the parsed value or a tolerance band instead of an exact string.

keyTakeaways: A test only has value if it's reproducible: same inputs, same result, so a failure signals a real regression rather than RNG.
Push toward determinism by pinning the exact dated model version, temperature 0, and a seed where the provider supports it.
Freeze the outside world with record/replay of tool outputs, and mock the model entirely when testing your own logic, not generation.
Bit-exact reproducibility is elusive: non-associative GPU floating-point, shifting provider infra, and silent model updates all leak.
Because temperature 0 is not a guarantee, assert on semantics and tolerances — parsed values, chosen tools, score bands — never exact strings.
